comments.text: Hey Product Hunt 👋I'm Yunhao, co-founder and CEO of TestSprite. More than 150,000 developers have built with TestSprite over the past three years.Your coding agent fixes one thing and breaks another. This year we met team after team that shipped with a coding agent and an AI reviewer while nobody really clicked through the product, and the bugs piled up until they went off together. So we built TestSprite 4.0, a brand-new testing agent that remembers what your app should do and checks all of it, every time.✍️ How it worksTell it what your app should do. Plain words are enough; a PRD, a Jira or Linear ticket, or your repo makes it sharper. When something is unclear, it asks instead of guessing.It explores your running app first. It maps the flows and plans coverage, then writes and runs end-to-end UI and API tests in real browsers, 100+ at once. It signs itself in (one-time codes included) and remembers your app between runs.It tells real bugs from noise. Every failure is sorted into a real bug, a test problem or an environment problem, with what should have happened, what happened, and a recording of each step.It keeps checking every change. Tests you approve become your regression suite. It maintains them as your UI changes, and what a test expects only changes with your approval. Run it from the web app, from your terminal with our open-source CLI (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or any coding agent can drive it), or on every pull request.📊 The numbers94% bug-finding accuracy on our benchmark, where Claude Code (Opus 5.5) and Codex (GPT-6.1 Sol) score 86%.~100× cheaper. Generating and running 200 UI integration tests costs $4.60 on TestSprite and $428 on GPT-6 Astra, at similar execution accuracy (96.5% vs 95.3%).🐛 What it caught in our own productWe test TestSprite with TestSprite. Before this launch it caught a delete dialog that never said which list it was about to delete, a search that told people "No test list created" while they had 11 lists, and a "Back to Home" button that sent signed-in users to our marketing site. Of the issues it raised that we've checked, 16 of 19 were important, and the other 3 were minor.🎉 Launch-day offer: sign up today and get your first month of the Starter plan free.What would you want an agent like this to catch before your next release? comments.text: Hey Product Hunt! I'm Elad, Principal Product Manager at Netlify.Over the last couple of years, millions of new builders have shown up on Netlify, driven by AI. I know it sounds like a cliche! but honestly, we’ve had a front row seat to this renaissance. And we saw an ever growing number of those wanting to ship use-case like multiplayer apps or live chat, collaborative spaces,rich data dashboards, and AI agents - some of which need to run long agentic loops with tools for minutes to hours.Those backends kept hitting the limits of functions, and our answer was usually "either adapt to our constraints, or - unfortunately - host that part of your app somewhere else." Of course, this never sat right with me (or any of us).So we built Netlify Server: a long-running server for your backend, with everything a server can do and none of the work of running one.To keep it concrete, here’s what having this server means in practice:Hold WebSockets open for real-time collaboration, games, and chatKeep connection pools, caches, and state in memory between requestsRun agent loops and long AI calls without racing to fit a timeoutBring many existing backend apps & tools as they are, with no adapters (with frameworks like Express, Hono, Koa, etc.)Servers have the same building lifecycle as other projects: you get deploy previews, you can roll back easily, and each branch gets its own Netlify Database branch. So you can safely test changes in isolation before you decide whether to publish any of them. Servers scale up with traffic, and scale to zero when nothing's using them.The team “Early Access” is probably selling it short tbh, because multiple teams within Netlify have been building with servers for a while - apps that we now use in our daily work. The team was also great just building cool examples. I made one or two, or more, myself 🙂Usage is free during Early Access. Start with the docs or just tell the agent in the Netlify UI what you want to create. We'd love to know what's the cool real-time / multiplayer / agent idea you've been holding off on!

Netlify has been one of my most used platforms this year due to just how easy it is to go from idea to fully working app in literally minutes. It's so good in fact that it stood up to my stress testing building and launching a new app, every day, for 30 days - TWICE! It's so easy to build and integrates seamlessly with the tools I already use. Plus it has an amazing community team and Netlify Server is just one more thing that makes it my go-to platform for everything from developing, hosting, and scaling all my projects. Congrats on the launch (and rebrand) team!

Congrats on shipping this. We run live game rooms where up to 300 phones answer the same question at once, so this is close to home. Hi, I’m Wade and I run product here at Netlify. Given the team has shared so many great details about Netlify Server, I thought I’d share three cool things at my pre-launch testing party for Netlify Server.1/ Quiver Hollow, a multiplayer archery game, where the server keeps both human and AI archers in sync, with everyone dodging arrows.2/ An OpenClaw agent I could chat with on Telegram where the server gives the agent time to work through a task before replying.3/ A holiday wish wall where you write a wish on a gift tag and hang it up for all to see. It’s a regular Node.js application whose Express backend could run as-is alongside the front end.We also used Netlify Server at our last board meeting.Our founder, Matt, had already shown us at an all-hands how much you could do by building the presentation as an app. We did the same thing for our board meeting. Hours before the meeting, we realized how many times we were having to say “next slide, please,” and so Matt updated the board app to let any/all presenters advance the slides from their own laptop. Behind the scenes, server kept a WebSocket open so that when someone went to change the slide, it changed for everyone at the same time.This is only scratching the surface and the potential. comments.text: Hey Product Hunt,I'm Ravi, co-founder of Scalekit. Today we're launching AgentKit, an MCP gateway that handles auth and tool-calling for AI agents in production.Why now? MCP standardized the interface, and any agent can now call Gmail or Salesforce after an afternoon of work.But the tool call is only the surface. Once an agent ships to real users, everything underneath it shows up:whose credentials each call executes withwhich tools each agent should have in contextthe internal systems no catalog coverswhat happens when an upstream API pushes backwho's accountable for every actionThat layer decides whether an agent makes it to production. It's what we built AgentKit for.Try it free: scalekit.com. The free tier includes 10,000 tool calls a month and all 600+ connectors. Make your first tool call from the dashboard, or start from your terminal with npx @ scalekit-inc/cli setup.Here's what it looks like in practice.Say you're shipping a sales agent inside your product. A rep types: "Prep me for the Acme renewal. Pull the deal, the last three email threads, what the team said in Slack, when we last met them, and how much they've used the product this quarter."Four apps, one ask. Getting it working for one rep in a demo is easy. Here's what's underneath when it runs for every rep at every customer:Thousands of OAuth grants, not four. 40 customers × 30 reps × Salesforce, Gmail, Slack and Calendar = 4,800 connected accounts. Each needs its tokens stored, isolated per customer, and refreshed before they expire mid-run. → AgentKit manages connected accounts end to end. Users authorize through an auth link you surface in your app. Tokens live in a per-tenant AES-256 vault, refresh automatically, and are injected at execution time. They never touch your code, logs, or prompts.Every call has to execute as the right user. The agent should see what that rep can see at that customer, and nothing more. Not a shared service account with org-wide access to every inbox. → Every tool call executes with the end user's own credentials, within the scopes they granted.Every tool definition costs context. Gmail alone exposes ~30 tools; four apps put over a hundred on the table. At ~200 tokens per definition, 40 tools burn ~8,000 tokens before the agent does any work, and tool selection gets worse as the list grows. Your prep agent needs about ten tools. Your outbound agent needs a different ten. → Virtual MCP Servers let you compose a tool set per agent role, across connectors. Each role gets one static MCP URL; you mint a short-lived session token per user per run. Smaller context and least-privilege access: ten tool definitions (~2,000 tokens) instead of over a hundred (20,000+).The data you need has no connector. Usage lives in your customer's internal analytics service. No catalog covers it, so you'd build that integration yourself, auth included. → Define it as a custom connector (OAuth 2.0, API key, bearer token, RSA or basic auth), or point AgentKit at a remote MCP server. It runs on the same gateway with the same credential handling and logs as the 600+ built-in connectors.It has to hold up and be auditable. Rate limits, timeouts, upstream errors the model can't act on. Then a deal stage changes and someone asks whether the rep did it or the agent did. → Retries and rate limits are handled on every call. Every call is logged with agent, user, tool and response, and logs stream to Datadog or Splunk.None of this shows up in a demo. All of it shows up in production. AgentKit handles that layer: 30,000+ tools across 600+ apps behind one MCP gateway. And with Triggers, an agent can start on its own the moment an email lands.Python and Node SDKs. Works with the Anthropic and OpenAI SDKs, LangChain, Google ADK, Vercel AI SDK, Mastra, and Claude Code. You keep your framework and backend.Which of these five has slowed your agent down the most?

Agentic tasks burn through tokens fast (Anthropic says so themselves), so that $200/month cap can disappear quicker than you'd expect. The agentic future is definitely coming, but "AI that can access everything" and "AI that keeps you in control" are two very different products for two very different users.
